Coco Bandero lies in the San Blas area and is a stop on island-hopping sea journeys. Clear water and reef areas offer opportunities to explore the underwater world close to shore. Colorful fish and corals can be found here, adding to the scenery around the island.

The stop is devoted to swimming, snorkeling and trips out on the water. From a yacht or kayak, you can take in the shallows and the outlines of the shoreline. Coco Bandero complements Panama's other islands with the same Caribbean combination of white sand, greenery and shades of blue, leaving time to relax by the sea.

Cocora Valley lies in the central range of the Colombian Andes, in the coffee-growing region near Salento. Quindío wax palms, Colombia's national tree, grow on its green slopes. Their slender trunks rise above pastures and patches of humid forest, making the palms visible across the valley.

Walking trails let you see the palms up close and discover the vegetation of the cloud forest. Both the sweeping views of the slopes and the small details are worth noticing: leaves, woodland plants and the changing landscape along the trail. A visit to the valley is often combined with stops in Salento and at coffee farms.

Colca is known for its deep canyon and mountain panoramas. Viewpoints reveal the terrain, offering a close look at the slopes and valley below. Traveling through this area shows another side of the Andes, with open vistas and dramatic changes in elevation across the landscape.

Cruz del Cóndor is one of the best-known places to observe Andean condors. The birds ride air currents over the canyon, making the chance to see them part of the nature-focused journey. Colca is often combined with Chivay and Arequipa, adding a mountain route to visits around the cities.
